summary: Defines a generic template for signed objects in the RPKI, which use the Cryptographic Message Syntax as the wrapper. Other RPKI object types, like ROAs and manifests, follow this template. It was later updated by RFC 9589.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6488 gives signed RPKI objects a shared format for carrying their data, signature and signer certificate. A relying party checks that format, verifies the signature and validates the certificate before using an object.

subtitle: The common CMS format and validation rules for signed RPKI objects.

tldr.problem: RPKI signed objects carry assertions beyond the resource data in certificates. Different object types need a consistent way to package and verify signatures.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6488 profiles the CMS SignedData structure, requiring DER encoding, one signer and one end-entity certificate, specified signed attributes, and checks for both the signature and certificate.
tldr.outcome: A separate Standards Track document defines each object's payload and any additional validation. RFC 6488 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9589.

today: RFC 6488 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9589. The unit metadata does not list an RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: A Shared Format for RPKI Assertions
sections.content:
The RPKI carries IP address and AS number resource information in X.509 certificates. Other assertions use signed objects, which are digitally signed data structures rather than certificates. RFC 6488 defines the common template for those objects using Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

The template specifies only properties shared by all signed object types. It does not define the payload for a particular object. A separate Standards Track document must define that payload and any additional validation steps; the RFC cites the Route Origination Authorization as an example.

CMS was selected as the encapsulation format to make use of existing software for processing CMS messages. The algorithms and key sizes used in RPKI are specified separately in RFC 6485.
sections.plainLanguage: RPKI signed objects share a common outer structure for their signatures and certificates. Each object type still needs its own specification for the data it contains.

sections.title: The CMS Signed-Data Profile
sections.content:
An RPKI signed object is a CMS SignedData object encoded with ASN.1 Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER). Its outer content type is id-signedData, with object identifier 1.2.840.113549.1.7.2. The SignedData version must be 3, and its digestAlgorithms set contains exactly one algorithm from the RPKI algorithm profile.

The certificates field is required and contains exactly one RPKI end-entity certificate. The crls field is omitted, and signerInfos contains exactly one SignerInfo. That SignerInfo also uses version 3, and its signer identifier is the SubjectKeyIdentifier from the included certificate.

The signed attributes must include content-type and message-digest, and may include signing-time or binary-signing-time. No other signed attributes are allowed, and unsigned attributes must be omitted. The eContentType and payload syntax are defined by the document for each object type.
sections.plainLanguage: The format allows one signer and one certificate, with required labels for the payload type and its digest. The payload itself depends on the kind of RPKI object.

sections.title: Validating a Signed Object
sections.content:
Before using a signed object, a relying party must check that its structure follows the profile. Among other checks, it verifies the SignedData type and version, the single certificate and matching signer identifier, required and permitted attributes, algorithm profile and DER encoding.

The relying party then verifies the signature using the public key in the included end-entity certificate and confirms that the certificate is valid in the RPKI, including a valid certification path from a trust anchor. Checks can be performed in any order.

If a generic check fails, the object must be discarded and treated as absent. Passing these checks is necessary but not enough: the relying party must also perform validation defined for that specific object type. An object stops being valid when its certificate expires or is revoked.
sections.plainLanguage: A relying party checks that the object follows the required format, that its signature matches, and that the signer certificate is valid. It discards an object if a check fails, then performs any checks required for that object type.

sections.title: Defining a Specific Signed Object
sections.content:
A new RPKI signed object must be defined in an Internet Standards Track document based on this profile. That document assigns one object identifier for both the eContentType and content-type attribute, defines the syntax of the eContent payload, and describes any extra validation a relying party must perform.

IANA maintains the RPKI Signed Objects registry with an informal object name, its eContentType identifier and a reference to its specification. RFC 6488 initially registers the ROA with OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.24 and the Manifest with OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.26.
sections.plainLanguage: A specification for a new object must say what its payload looks like and what extra checks it needs. IANA records the object's name, identifier and defining specification.

sections.title: Integrity Without Confidentiality
sections.content:
The RFC makes no confidentiality assumption for signed object data and expects repositories to be publicly accessible. A signature provides integrity and authenticity when it verifies and the end-entity certificate is validated.

Because the objects use CMS for encapsulation, the CMS security considerations also apply. The template does not replace validation specific to a signed object type.
sections.plainLanguage: These objects are expected to be public. Their signatures help a relying party check who signed the data and whether it has changed.
